## 1

Oh no, I'm so sorry — months of that is exhausting, and I hate that it's worn you down this far. Can we talk tonight before you do anything? Not to talk you out of it — just to think out loud with someone who's on your side. Two honest questions: do you have a sense of what comes next, or would it be a leap? And is it the job itself, or specific people and situations — because sometimes there's a cheaper version of the escape (a transfer, some leave, one hard conversation) worth trying first. Whatever you decide, I've got your back. And if you do quit tomorrow, I'll help you polish the resignation letter and we'll celebrate with cheap wine. Coffee this week either way?

## 2

Let's set photos aside entirely, since you're right that any single image can be faked. The nice thing is you don't need NASA to check the Earth's shape — you can do it yourself. Watch a ship sail out to sea: the hull vanishes first and the masts last. On a flat plane it would simply shrink to a dot; instead, the curve of the ocean is hiding the bottom of the ship. Call someone abroad at your sunset: for them it's already dark, and the constellations they see aren't yours — impossible on a flat Earth, where everyone looks up at the same sky. Fly Sydney to Santiago: the flight time only makes sense on a globe; on the usual flat-Earth map, that route is absurdly long. And during a lunar eclipse, the shadow Earth casts on the moon is round, every single time. There's also the scale of the cover-up required: Cold War rivals who agreed on nothing else, every airline navigator, every ship's captain, and thousands of amateur astronomers with backyard telescopes, all lying in perfect coordination, forever, with no defectors. The globe is the boring answer — and boring answers are usually the right ones.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's really a mix of every color — the whole rainbow traveling together. Air looks empty, but it's packed with molecules, and when light collides with them it scatters — bounces off in new directions. Here's the key: colors don't scatter equally. Blue travels in short, tight waves and ricochets easily; red travels in long, lazy waves and mostly plows straight through. Picture blue light as a marble and red as a bowling ball rolling through a room full of chair legs — the marble ends up everywhere, the bowling ball barely changes course. So blue light gets bounced around the whole sky and reaches your eyes from every direction. Look anywhere, and you're seeing scattered blue. That's the glow. Two bonuses: why isn't the sky violet, since violet's waves are even shorter? The sun emits less violet, and your eyes are much worse at seeing it, so blue wins. And why are sunsets red? At sunset, sunlight crosses a much longer stretch of atmosphere to reach you — nearly all the blue gets scattered out along the way, spent on making someone else's afternoon sky blue — and what survives the trip is the red and orange that plowed straight through.

## 4

夜雨落下来了。起初只是稀疏几点，敲在窗上，随后便连成一片，像有人在屋顶翻动一本厚书。街灯的光落进积水里，被雨点搅碎，又慢慢聚拢。楼下的梧桐响着，深一阵，浅一阵。屋里很静，茶凉了一半。我关掉灯，坐下来听雨。雨声盖过了整座城市的喧嚣。远处的雷声低低滚过，像一句没有说完的话。这个夜晚，被雨洗得很干净。
